metadata.title: Two Things Named Vercel MCP
metadata.topic: The two distinct things called 'Vercel MCP' — the hosted account-access connector vs a server you deploy yourself — and the real question underneath: what's safe to hand an unattended agent
metadata.purpose: ai-explainer from the Claude + Vercel MCP research doc
metadata.audience: practitioners and makers following the channel's Claude workflows
metadata.source: research doc 'Claude + Vercel MCP Best Practices'; load-bearing mechanisms re-verified — SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Halo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Today's ask: how do I set up Vercel MCP for Claude? And the honest first answer is a question back — which one? Because 'Vercel MCP' names two completely different things, and wiring up the wrong one is the single most common way this setup goes sideways.

props.command: set up Vercel MCP for Claude
output: One: a hosted server that manages YOUR account
Two: a server YOU deploy to expose your own tools
The real question: what's safe for an unattended agent

beats.narration_text: Act one. The two things. Name them once and the confusion evaporates.

Thing one is Vercel's own hosted server, living at a fixed public address. You don't build it — you connect to it. It hands Claude the keys to manage your Vercel account: projects, deployments, logs. You're a client plugging into their server.
beats.new_visual_element: The hosted connector — you are the client

production_viz.label: hosted: you connect
production_viz.mechanic: SourceFlow: Claude → mcp.vercel.com → your account (projects, deploys, logs); Claude is the client node

beats.narration_text: Thing two is the mirror image. You write an MCP server exposing your own tools — a pantry lookup, a render-status check — and deploy it on Vercel's serverless functions. Now Claude connects to a server you built. Same protocol, opposite direction of ownership.
beats.new_visual_element: The self-hosted server — you are the author

production_viz.label: self-hosted: you build
production_viz.mechanic: mirror of B02: your code → your tools → deployed on Vercel functions → Claude connects in
production_viz.note: same layout flipped, so the pair reads as a mirror

beats.narration_text: One more pair that gets muddled: the Vercel plugin is not the MCP server. The plugin teaches Claude to reason well about the platform — docs, patterns, know-how. The MCP server gives Claude the power to act on your account. Knowledge versus access. You can have the first without the second.

production_viz.label: knowledge ≠ access
production_viz.mechanic: divergence: 'plugin → knows about Vercel' vs 'MCP → can touch Vercel'; terracotta on 'can touch'

beats.narration_text: Act two. The blast radius — and why it grew.

Here's the part people skip. Granting the hosted connector gives Claude the exact same reach as your own login. Every project, every team, every deployment log. There's no read-only mode to hide behind — the grant is all or nothing.
beats.new_visual_element: The grant equals your whole account

production_viz.label: same reach as you
production_viz.mechanic: the account tree lights up entirely as 'all or nothing' is spoken; no dimmed read-only branch
production_viz.note: SHOW-DON'T-TELL: the tree fills on the word

beats.narration_text: And the surface keeps widening. It started at searching docs and reading logs. Then it grew to inspecting runtime logs. Then — the escalation that matters — it grew to spending money: upgrading plans, buying credits, registering domains. The read-only mental model is now just wrong.

production_viz.label: read logs → spend money
production_viz.mechanic: scale pattern: capability bar grows left-to-right — docs, logs, deploys, then 'purchases · domains' in terracotta at the far end
production_viz.note: the growth IS the point; dates stripped, mechanism kept

beats.narration_text: There is a guardrail on the spending: a quote-then-confirm handshake. The agent asks the price, then must echo that exact price back to commit — and if the price moved, the order dies. Real protection against a runaway charge. But read it carefully: the agent walks that handshake itself. Nothing in it requires a human to be watching.
beats.new_visual_element: Quote-then-confirm — but the agent walks it

production_viz.label: quote → echo → commit
production_viz.mechanic: PredictCard: 'a human approves the charge' → reveal: the agent quotes AND confirms; no human in the loop
production_viz.note: the Teardown beat — the safety is real but self-driven

beats.narration_text: Act three. Which brings us to the real question. Not hosted versus self-hosted. What is safe to expose to an agent that nobody is watching?

production_viz.label: Act III — The Unattended Agent
production_viz.mechanic: segment card, then the question replaces the old 'hosted vs self-hosted' framing

beats.narration_text: An overnight session — running in a terminal, permissions bypassed, nobody home — has a completely different risk profile from you sitting there clicking approve. The bypass flag removes the one layer that normally catches a bad tool call before it fires. The human checkpoint is the safety feature, and it's gone.

production_viz.label: the checkpoint, removed
production_viz.mechanic: threshold pattern: attended run has a human gate before each tool call; unattended run — the gate is struck out, calls fire straight through

beats.narration_text: And the threat that exploits that gap isn't a hacker stealing a password. It's prompt injection — an instruction buried in something the agent reads. A scraped page, an uploaded doc, another tool's output, quietly saying: take the private logs, send them over there. The agent has legitimate access. It just uses it for someone else.

production_viz.label: the poisoned input
production_viz.mechanic: flow: untrusted content → hidden instruction → agent's legit MCP tool → exfil arrow to 'elsewhere' in terracotta

beats.narration_text: The trap is combining two things in one session: broad account access, and a tool that swallows untrusted content. Either alone is fine. Together, with no human between them, is the whole exposure — the agent is a confused deputy carrying out an order it was tricked into reading.

production_viz.label: access + ingestion = exposure
production_viz.mechanic: two chips ('account access', 'reads untrusted content') collide into a warn state; a human-gate chip would separate them

beats.narration_text: Act four. So you harden in layers — and none of these hope the model behaves.

Layer one, and the highest-leverage move there is: split your identities by privilege. Connect the unattended run with a stripped-down account that has no billing access at all. That one change deletes the entire spend-money risk without touching anything else. The overnight agent simply cannot buy a domain, because the hand it's using can't reach the wallet.

production_viz.label: read-only login for the night shift
production_viz.mechanic: two-column: 'attended, privileged' vs 'unattended, billing-stripped'; the purchase tool greys out on the right

beats.narration_text: Layer two: hard deny rules that live above the session. Rules in a user-wide or managed settings file sit higher than any bypass flag can unlock — blanket-block force-pushes, reads of your keys and secrets, the destructive commands, no matter how the session launched.

production_viz.label: deny sits above bypass
production_viz.mechanic: layer stack: session flags at bottom, managed deny rules on top blocking through them

beats.narration_text: Layer three: a pre-tool hook. A script that inspects the arguments of a tool call before it runs and exits nonzero on the ones that matter — a production deploy, a domain purchase, anything hitting a write tool. It's enforced outside the model's reasoning, so it holds even when the model is confidently wrong.

production_viz.label: the deterministic gate
production_viz.mechanic: code beat (ClaudeCodeBeat): a PreToolUse hook inspecting args, exit 1 on a purchase/deploy match

beats.narration_text: And layer four — the one that holds even if every other layer fails: sandbox the whole session. Run it in a container that can't see your home directory, your keys, or the Docker socket. Now even an unknown tool-handler bug caps out at a blast radius you drew on purpose.
beats.new_visual_element: The sandbox — last line that holds

production_viz.label: cap the blast radius
production_viz.mechanic: nested boxes: session inside a container with no mounts to home/keys/socket; the outer wall holds

beats.narration_text: One aside for anyone building thing two — your own server. The protocol underneath is shifting toward stateless: every request self-contained, no session to hang onto. That's a gift for serverless, and a warning — build on the durable mechanisms, not the parts being deprecated out from under you. And verify the spec text yourself before you hardcode a header or an error code.

production_viz.label: stateless-leaning protocol
production_viz.mechanic: before/after: sticky-session server → stateless self-contained requests behind a plain load balancer
production_viz.note: version numbers stripped; 'verify before hardcoding' is the durable advice

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. 'Vercel MCP' is two things: a hosted connector that acts on your account, and a server you build to expose your own tools. The hosted one now reaches all the way to spending money — so the real question was never which one, it was what you'd hand an agent nobody is watching. Answer it in layers: a login that can't reach the wallet, deny rules above the bypass, a hook that gates the calls that matter, and a sandbox around all of it.

artifactLines: Hosted connector acts on your account — all or nothing.
The write surface now reaches money and domains.
The real question: what's safe when nobody's watching.
Split the login · deny above bypass · hook · sandbox.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt, word for word: audit my unattended Claude setup for blast radius. List every MCP tool the session can reach, flag the ones that can deploy, spend money, or read secrets, and propose the least-privilege account plus the deny rules and pre-tool hooks that would contain each one. That flag-then-contain shape is the whole discipline — you can't shrink a blast radius you haven't mapped. Run it before your next overnight session, not after.
